output.brief: The jump in write-offs is mostly an internal handling problem, not Haverlow's fault. Haverlow's trailers held 2–3.5°C at door-open, and the chambers held 2–4°C. Since 27 July the night receiving team has been cut from six to four, and pallets now wait a median of about 3h52 on an unrefrigerated dock (15–17°C) before going into a chamber. They used to wait 44 minutes. Night write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9% across all suppliers, while day-shift rates stayed flat. The receipt probe readings of 6.5–8°C were taken after that wait, so they don't show how the product arrived. A chargeback and a volume shift to Pellridge would punish the wrong party, and Pellridge's night-received product is hit just as hard. Next step: restore night staffing to six and set a maximum dock-to-chamber time, tracked weekly from scan data. Keep the receipt probe. Also reverse the saving that CR-2231 booked (£2,300 a week), since it is dwarfed by the extra write-offs. Corriebank's looser credit rules probably explain part of the rise in customer credits, but the evidence is thin. Ask for their claim-level data and reconcile a sample before changing terms. I am fairly confident in the main conclusion. The Corriebank share is unproven.
